status: drafted via multi-agent workflow grounded in the real extracted verse text, adversarially fact-checked and corrected
notes: Grounded directly in E:/Unity/Clicker_Genesis/Assets/Resources/Verses/Ethiopian/proverbs_30.json — read in full (all 31 chapters, 915 verses). Real finding, stated plainly rather than assumed: this Ethiopian-translation Proverbs is textually and structurally IDENTICAL in content/organization to the standard KJV-tradition Proverbs — same 31 chapters, same three authorial seams (Solomon's own two collections at 1:1 and 10:1, plus the men of Hezekiah's later copied-out collection explicitly named at 25:1), the same distinct non-Solomonic voices (Agur son of Jakeh, ch.30; King Lemuel and his mother's teaching, 31:1-9), and the same closing acrostic praising the virtuous woman (31:10-31). Unlike this project's own Ethiopian Ezra (a genuinely different 9-chapter text matching the 1 Esdras tradition), Proverbs in this translation shows NO deuterocanonical additions, no reordering, and no missing/extra material versus the familiar KJV shape — verified by reading the actual chapter-by-chapter text (1-9 read in full, 10-31 read in full, including the Hezekiah-scribe seam at 25:1, Agur's oracle at 30:1-33, and Lemuel's oracle/the virtuous-woman poem at 31:1-31) rather than assumed from the book's familiar name. Because Proverbs is wisdom literature, not narrative, most of its 'characters' are literary personifications or recurring themes rather than people with genealogies — following the same law/theme-tier pattern used for Leviticus and Deuteronomy in the KJV index, since these sections are content/teaching-driven (deliveredBy Solomon in every case except the Virtuous Woman poem, delivered by Lemuel relaying his mother) rather than personally-embodied narrative. No scripture-stated ages exist anywhere in this book, so every ageEvents array is empty by design. Naming note: 'Ithiel and Ucal,' addressed in Agur's oracle (30:1), take no independent action in the text and are not given entries; an unrelated same-named Ithiel appears only in a much later, unconnected genealogy elsewhere in scripture and is not the same person — flagged, not merged. IDs are suffixed _ethiopian_proverbs throughout to avoid any collision with the existing KJV CharacterIndex's Proverbs.json ids (which use bare names like 'solomon,' 'agur_son_of_jakeh') or with a future Geneva-translation Proverbs file.

characters.name: Solomon

verses.note: The proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel.
The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son is the heaviness of his mother.
These are also proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out.

funFacts: Three separate headings across the book credit Solomon by name (1:1, 10:1, 25:1) — the book is explicitly a compilation of multiple Solomonic collections, not one continuous composition.

Proverbs 25:1 is the book's own account of scribal transmission — 'the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out' a Solomonic collection generations after it was first spoken, the direct real-world precedent behind this game's whole Scribes system.

characters.name: Wisdom
characters.purpose: Personifies wisdom as a woman crying out publicly in the streets and city gates, warning that those who refuse her call will be abandoned to their own calamity, and describing her own presence beside the LORD from before creation — establishing wisdom as something openly offered, moral, and worth pursuing above silver or gold.

verses.note: Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets... in the openings of the gates.
Doth not wisdom cry? and understanding put forth her voice? She standeth in the top of high places.
The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old.
Wisdom hath builded her house, she hath hewn out her seven pillars... she hath also furnished her table.

funFacts: Wisdom's house with 'her seven pillars' (9:1) is deliberately echoed a few verses later when the foolish woman also 'sitteth at the door of her house' (9:14) — the two personifications are set up as direct opposites.

characters.name: The Strange Woman / Folly
characters.purpose: A recurring warning, personified as a seductive 'strange woman' whose house 'inclineth unto death,' against adultery and moral folly — culminating in an extended first-person narrative scene (ch.7) of a naive young man being lured to ruin, and closing with a mirrored 'foolish woman' who calls out from her own door (9:13-18) opposite Wisdom's.

verses.note: To deliver thee from the strange woman... For her house inclineth unto death, and her paths unto the dead.
the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb... But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a twoedged sword.
by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life.
extended narrative of a young man 'void of understanding' met by a woman 'with the attire of an harlot' at twilight, ending 'as an ox goeth to the slaughter.'
A foolish woman is clamourous... he knoweth not that the dead are there, and that her guests are in the depths of hell.

funFacts: Folly's line 'Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant' (9:17) is a deliberate ironic mirror of Wisdom's own invitation to 'eat of my bread, and drink of the wine' only two verses earlier (9:5).

characters.name: The Fear of the LORD
characters.purpose: The book's programmatic refrain, opening the main collection, repeated as a summary statement mid-book, and closing the entire book — establishing that reverent submission to God, not raw intellect, is the necessary foundation for all true wisdom and knowledge.

verses.note: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.

funFacts: The refrain brackets the whole book almost exactly — the opening line of the main collection (1:7) and the final praised quality of the closing poem (31:30) are the same theme.

characters.name: The Sluggard
characters.purpose: Uses vivid imagery — the diligent ant needing 'no guide, overseer, or ruler,' an overgrown thorn-choked field, a door turning on its hinges — to warn against laziness and its inevitable end in poverty.

verses.note: Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, Provideth her meat in the summer.
How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?... So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man.
I went by the field of the slothful... it was all grown over with thorns, and nettles had covered the face thereof.

funFacts: 'Go to the ant, thou sluggard' (6:6) is one of the single most quoted lines in the entire book.

characters.name: Agur

verses.note: The words of Agur the son of Jakeh, even the prophecy: the man spake unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal.
Surely I am more brutish than any man... I neither learned wisdom, nor have the knowledge of the holy.
four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise — the ants, the conies, the locusts, and the spider.

funFacts: Agur's opening self-description as 'more brutish than any man' (30:2) is a distinct, humble authorial voice, unlike Solomon's confident royal instruction elsewhere in the book.
His 'three things... yea, four' numerical sayings (30:15-31) are a literary form that appears nowhere else in Proverbs.

Naming collision flagged, not merged: 'Ithiel,' one of the two men Agur addresses (30:1), shares his name with an unrelated man listed generations later in a separate genealogy elsewhere in scripture — the text gives no indication they are the same person.

characters.name: King Lemuel

verses.note: The words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him.
It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink wine... lest they drink, and forget the law, and pervert the judgment of any of the afflicted.
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction... plead the cause of the poor and needy.

funFacts: Lemuel is otherwise unidentified anywhere else in this translation — no genealogy, kingdom, or further appearance beyond these nine verses.
His oracle (31:1-9) transitions directly into the acrostic poem of the virtuous woman (31:10-31); the text itself only explicitly attributes the first nine verses to his mother's teaching.

characters.name: Lemuel's Mother

verses.note: What, my son? and what, the son of my womb? and what, the son of my vows?
Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings.

funFacts: She is the only mother in the book explicitly credited by the text as the direct source of an entire recorded section of instruction (31:1).

characters.name: The Virtuous Woman
characters.purpose: A closing poem praising an ideal capable wife — her trade, diligence, generosity to the poor, and reverence for God — following directly after Lemuel's mother's recorded teaching and closing the whole book on fear of the LORD (31:30) rather than beauty or status.

verses.note: Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.
She seeketh wool, and flax, and worketh willingly with her hands.
She considereth a field, and buyeth it: with the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard.
She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy.
Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.

funFacts: It closes the book on the same theme that opened it: fear of the LORD (compare 1:7 and 31:30).

genealogyLists.note: Bulk/unresolved references, kept out of the character list above.

ithiel_and_ucal.note: Two men Agur's oracle is addressed to; the text gives no independent action, genealogy, or further detail for either, so no separate character entry is made. A different, unrelated man also named Ithiel appears far later in an unconnected genealogical list elsewhere in scripture — flagged as a naming collision, not the same person.
